summary: Describes an extension to IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration under which hosts generate temporary addresses with randomized interface identifiers. Changing addresses over time limits how long eavesdroppers and others can use the address to track a device.

plainLanguage.summary: Your computer wears a changing disguise for its address, so people watching can not easily follow it around the Internet.

questions: how long do ipv6 temporary addresses last
how are temporary ipv6 interface identifiers generated
subtitle: How IPv6 hosts generate short-lived, random addresses so outside observers cannot easily follow them around.

tldr.problem: Addresses built by SLAAC contain an interface identifier that can stay the same for a long time, which lets eavesdroppers and log collectors correlate unrelated activity from one host.
tldr.mechanism: A host adds temporary addresses made from a prefix plus a randomized interface identifier, with a limited lifetime (1 day preferred, 2 days valid by default), and keeps replacing them with new ones.
tldr.outcome: The window in which activity can be trivially correlated by address shrinks. The RFC obsoletes RFC 4941 and notes it does not stop sophisticated traffic analysis.

today: RFC 8981 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2021. It obsoletes RFC 4941, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Privacy Problem with Stable Addresses
sections.content:
IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC, RFC 4862) usually gives a host stable addresses made of a network prefix from a local router plus a locally generated interface identifier (IID). Because the IID is embedded in the address, it cannot be hidden, and anytime a fixed identifier is used in many contexts, unrelated activity can be correlated.

The RFC names two correlators: an attacker on the path who sees addresses in datagrams, and an attacker who can read the logs of the peers the host talked to. Even when payloads are encrypted, addresses in packet headers appear in the clear, so a laptop that visits several networks could be followed from place to place.

This document specifies an extension to SLAAC that generates temporary addresses to help mitigate this. It is a revision of RFC 4941 and formally obsoletes it.
sections.plainLanguage: If you always wore the same bright red hat, anyone could follow you around town. Changing hats often makes you harder to follow.

sections.title: Limits of the Idea
sections.content:
The RFC is frank about what changing the IID cannot do. The network prefix is also a constant identifier: all hosts at a home share it. If a network has very few hosts, perhaps just one, changing only the IID does not enhance privacy. Other identifiers also persist, such as DNS names and the cookies exchanged by web browsers and servers.

Temporary addresses will not stop an on-path attacker from correlating by unencrypted payload contents or by packet size and timing, nor stop an on-link observer such as the host's default router from tracking all its addresses.

The approach fits SLAAC: change the IID over time. A host acting as a server may keep a stable address tied to its name, while a temporary address shields its identity when it initiates communication. The generation algorithm needs an input that is unpredictable to outside observers.
sections.plainLanguage: A new hat does not help if you are the only person in a tiny village, or if you keep walking past the same cameras in the same coat.

sections.title: Design Guidelines for Temporary Addresses
sections.content:
Temporary addresses are typically used for outgoing sessions and for a short time (typically hours to days), after which they are deprecated. A deprecated address can still serve established connections but is not used to start new ones. New temporary addresses are generated to replace ones that expire.

Lifetimes must be limited and statistically different from address to address, so that it is hard to predict when a new address will appear. By default one address is generated per prefix advertised by SLAAC, and the IIDs must be statistically different across prefixes and interfaces. They must be hard to predict even if the algorithm and earlier IIDs are known, and must be semantically opaque with no specific patterns.

The RFC assumes that hosts can prefer temporary addresses over stable ones for outgoing communication, as RFC 6724 requires implementations to allow, and that applications may be able to override the default through an API such as the one in RFC 5014.
sections.plainLanguage: Each disguise is used for a day or so, only for starting new conversations, and no two disguises look related.

sections.title: Generating Randomized Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
Two example algorithms are given. The simple one takes bits from a pseudorandom number generator (see RFC 4086 for randomness requirements). The second augments RFC 7217 so a host can use one algorithm for both stable and temporary addresses. It computes RID = F(Prefix, Net_Iface, Network_ID, Time, DAD_Counter, secret_key), where F() is a pseudorandom function that must not be computable without the secret key and must be hard to reverse. BLAKE3 and HMAC-SHA-256 are named as options, and HMAC-MD5 is called unacceptable.

The secret_key SHOULD be at least 128 bits, must be initialized to a pseudorandom number at bootstrap, and MUST NOT be used for anything else, including generating stable addresses. Using the MAC address for Net_Iface means regenerating a randomized MAC address yields a different temporary address.

In both algorithms the resulting IID MUST be checked against the reserved IIDs and the IIDs already used on the same interface and prefix. If it is unacceptable, a new one is generated (in the second algorithm by incrementing DAD_Counter).
sections.plainLanguage: The computer rolls dice (or mixes a secret recipe) to invent a new name for itself, and re-rolls if the name is already taken or reserved.

sections.title: Creating, Expiring and Regenerating Addresses
sections.content:
When a Router Advertisement carries a Prefix Information option with the A bit set, the host processes it as in RFC 4862 and then, if it has no temporary address for that prefix, SHOULD create one. Each new address gets a random DESYNC_FACTOR. Its valid lifetime is the lower of the prefix's Valid Lifetime and TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME, and its preferred lifetime is the lower of the prefix's Preferred Lifetime and TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME - DESYNC_FACTOR. The address is formed by appending a randomized IID to the prefix, and the host MUST perform Duplicate Address Detection. After TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES consecutive failures it MUST log a system error and SHOULD NOT try again for that prefix on that interface.

When a temporary address becomes deprecated, a new one MUST be generated. The host SHOULD start REGEN_ADVANCE time units before deprecation so a preferred address is always available. When an interface connects to a different link, existing temporary addresses MUST be removed and new ones generated.

Implementations MUST let the end user enable or disable temporary addresses, and SHOULD let administrators do so, including per prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Whenever the router announces a neighborhood, the computer makes a fresh disguise for it, checks nobody else uses it, and swaps in a new one a little before the old one expires.

sections.title: Protocol Parameters and Defaults
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few variables. TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME defaults to 2 days and TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME to 1 day; users should be able to override both, and the preferred lifetime MUST be smaller than the valid lifetime. MAX_DESYNC_FACTOR is 0.4 times TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME, which yields statistically different lifetimes and at most three concurrent temporary addresses with the defaults. TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES defaults to 3.

REGEN_ADVANCE is 2 + (TEMP_IDGEN_RETRIES * DupAddrDetectTransmits * RetransTimer / 1000), which allows for time spent in DAD in the worst case. DESYNC_FACTOR is a random value between 0 and MAX_DESYNC_FACTOR, and it must be smaller than TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME - REGEN_ADVANCE.
sections.plainLanguage: Each disguise lasts about a day, can still be used for old conversations for two days, and a bit of randomness stops everyone's disguises from changing at the same moment.

sections.title: Side Effects and Changes from RFC 4941
sections.content:
Privacy can conflict with operations. Changing addresses makes packet traces and troubleshooting harder, may add Neighbor Discovery traffic if neighbor caches are small, and may make some security devices wrongly infer address forging. Some servers refuse clients whose address cannot be mapped to a DNS name, and some applications cope badly if an address becomes invalid while in use. Because IIDs of all temporary addresses must now differ, a host on a network with several prefixes may need to join more solicited-node multicast groups.

Compared with RFC 4941, this document fixes flaws such as the use of MD5 and reusing one IID across prefixes, allows hosts to use only temporary addresses, removes the recommendation that temporary addresses be disabled by default, reduces the default maximum valid lifetime from 1 week to 2 days (typically from 7 concurrent temporary addresses to 3), computes DESYNC_FACTOR for every address, relaxes the no-retry rule after repeated DAD failures from MUST NOT to SHOULD NOT, and incorporates errata.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing disguises protects you but makes life harder for the people who keep order, and the new rules fix some mistakes of the old version.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If very few hosts use a prefix for long periods, changing only the IID may not be enough, since the prefix is a constant identifier. The procedures work best when the prefix is reasonably nonstatic or used by many hosts. If a user authenticates in a session using a temporary address, privacy for that address is compromised for whoever receives the authentication information.

The method is believed to be ineffective against sophisticated traffic analysis; the RFC points to more advanced techniques such as onion routing. Frequent new addresses may also make it harder for ingress and egress filtering to tell legitimate temporary addresses from spoofed in-prefix source addresses, which can be addressed with per-address access control at some cost. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: A disguise will not help if you sign your real name, and a very clever watcher can still sometimes work out who you are.

items.title: Desync factor
items.text: Random, up to 0.4 times the preferred lifetime.
